mainTopic: How a בכור becomes holy: רב הונא's retroactive holiness, counting the majority of limbs, and what counts as the fetus 'opening the womb'.
overview: The amud opens by finishing an explanation of why the argument between רב הונא and רבה, about whether a בכור becomes holy retroactively, had to be stated in two cases. The גמרא then challenges רב הונא from a משנה that lets a person cut up a stuck firstborn limb by limb and throw the pieces to dogs. It answers that the משנה means each limb is thrown away right away, and it reads the משנה's later clause as limiting the first case. Next, רבא asks whether we follow the majority within a limb when half the fetus is out. A proof from the משנה's words 'most of it came out' is pushed off. רבא then asks a series of questions about unusual births: a fetus wrapped in palm fiber, a robe, another animal's afterbirth, or a hand, a fetus swallowed by a weasel, and two wombs pressed together. All of these end in תיקו. Finally, רב אחא, מר בר רב אשי and רבי ירמיה ask about womb walls that were widened, uprooted, or thinned. רבי זירא shows from an earlier question that thinned walls clearly do not make the fetus holy.

steps.title: Why the argument had to be stated in both cases
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes explaining why the argument between רב הונא and רבה needed to be taught in two separate cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: If we had only heard the argument in that case, we would think רבה says 'from now on' only there. But in this case, we would say he agrees with רב הונא. So both cases were needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wraps up its explanation of why the argument between רב הונא and רבה appears in two cases. Each case teaches something the other could not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In one case (one third came out through the side of the womb), saying 'holy from now on' is the stricter result, so רבה might hold it only there. In the other case (one third came out, then it was sold to a non-Jew), saying 'from now on' is the more lenient result, so we might think רבה agrees with רב הונא. Recording both cases shows that רבה holds his view either way.

keyTerms.meaning: It is necessary: both statements are needed and neither is extra
In this case / in that case

steps.confusionAlert: Both 'בְּהָא' (that case) and 'בְּהָא' (this case) look exactly the same. The context tells you which of the two earlier cases each one points to.

phrases.english: And if it had been stated only in that case:
phrases.notes: He means the earlier case where a third of the animal came out through the side wall of the womb.

phrases.english: in that case Rabba says it becomes holy from now on,
but in this case,
phrases.notes: This is the case where a third came out and then the animal was sold to a non-Jew.

phrases.english: I would say he agrees with Rav Huna;
therefore it is necessary to state both.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the צריכותא begun before this section.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבה holds 'holy from now on' in both cases, whether that leads to a stricter or a more lenient result.

steps.title: Challenge to רב הונא from cutting up a stuck firstborn
steps.stepSummary: A משנה allows throwing the limbs of a stuck firstborn to the dogs. If holiness is retroactive, the limbs should need burial.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned: an animal giving birth to a firstborn that is having trouble: one cuts it up limb by limb and throws the pieces to the dogs. Doesn't this mean he cuts and leaves the pieces lying until most of it is out? If you say it becomes holy retroactively, the משנה should have said the limbs must be buried!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a משנה to attack רב הונא, who holds that a בכור becomes holy retroactively.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא assumes the משנה means the cut limbs are left lying until most of the animal is out. Under רב הונא, once most of it has come out, all the earlier limbs would become holy retroactively. Holy limbs cannot be thrown to dogs; they must be buried. Since the משנה permits the dogs, this seems to go against רב הונא.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal giving birth to its firstborn
Having a hard time giving birth
Cuts it up limb by limb
Isn't it that...? (the גמרא suggests how to read a source)
Retroactively, going back to the beginning
It must be buried (the rule for holy things that cannot be used)

phrases.english: We learned: An animal giving birth to a firstborn that is having difficulty giving birth:
one cuts it up limb by limb
and throws the pieces to the dogs.
Isn't it that he cuts and leaves the pieces lying?
And if you say it is holy retroactively,
it should have said: it must be buried!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the צריכותא to a direct challenge against רב הונא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's view that a בכור becomes holy retroactively
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the cut limbs were left until most of the animal emerged, retroactive holiness would make them holy. The משנה should then require burial, yet it permits throwing them to dogs.

steps.title: The משנה means each limb is thrown away right after it is cut
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא defends רב הונא: the משנה is talking about someone who throws each limb away immediately.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. What case are we dealing with here? One who cuts and throws each piece away right away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by reading the משנה differently: each limb is thrown out as soon as it is cut.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If each limb is gone before most of the animal has come out, there is never a moment when 'most of it is born.' So retroactive holiness never takes hold of those limbs, and they may go to the dogs even according to רב הונא.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (used to narrow a source to a specific case)

phrases.english: No. What case are we dealing with here?
With one who cuts and throws each piece away immediately.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 2 by narrowing the משנה's case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה meant cutting and leaving the limbs until most of the animal emerged.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה means cutting and throwing each limb away immediately, so holiness never takes hold.

steps.title: Then the משנה should have taught the other case right there
steps.stepSummary: If cutting and leaving would require burial, the משנה should have said so within its first case, not in a separate later clause.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if one cuts and leaves the pieces, what then? They must be buried? If so, instead of teaching in the last part, 'If most of it came out, it must be buried, and the mother is free from the firstborn rule,' the משנה should have made the distinction inside the first case itself: 'When is this said? When one cuts and throws away limb by limb. But if he cuts and leaves them, they must be buried.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer: if your reading is right, the משנה chose a strange way to teach the rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the answer, the case of 'cutting and leaving' would require burial. That is a clear, useful case the משנה could have taught as a distinction inside its first ruling. Instead, the משנה teaches burial only in a separate clause, where most of the animal came out. This suggests that 'cutting and leaving' does not require burial, which brings the challenge against רב הונא back.

keyTerms.meaning: The later clause of a משנה
The mother is now free from the firstborn rule (any later births are not a בכור)
Let it make the distinction and teach it within the same case
When is this said? (a formula that limits a rule)

steps.confusionAlert: This step argues from the משנה's wording. If 'cut and leave' really needed burial, the משנה would have said so inside its first case. Since it didn't, the step 3 answer is in doubt, and step 5 answers this.

phrases.english: But if one cuts and leaves the pieces, what is the law? They must be buried?
Instead of teaching in the later clause:
"If most of it came out, it must be buried,
and the mother is exempt from the firstborn rule,"
let it make the distinction and teach it within that same case:
When is this said?
When one cuts and throws away limb by limb;
but if one cuts and leaves them, they must be buried.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 3 based on how the משנה is worded.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the משנה speaks only of cutting and throwing away immediately
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If cutting and leaving would require burial, the משנה should have taught that distinction inside its first case. Its silence suggests no such distinction exists.
steps.whyThisMatters: This argument from silence keeps the challenge to רב הונא alive. The next step (step 5) answers it.

steps.title: The later clause explains the first case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה's later clause is not a separate ruling. It explains when the first case applies: only when the limbs are thrown away right away. If they are left, they need burial.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes, that is exactly what the משנה means: When is this said? When he cuts and throws away. But if he cuts and leaves the limbs, it is as if most of the animal came out, and it must be buried.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 4. The later clause of the משנה is really explaining the first case, not adding a new one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 asked why the משנה didn't make this distinction inside its first case. The answer is that it did: the later line works like 'when is this said?', limiting the first ruling to someone who cuts and throws right away. When the limbs are left there, they add up to 'most of the animal came out', so the animal becomes holy and the limbs need burial, just as רב הונא holds.

keyTerms.meaning: In what case is this said? A phrase that limits an earlier ruling
Cuts off a limb and throws it away right away
Cuts off a limb and leaves it there
It must be buried, since it became holy

steps.whatToRemember: Throwing each limb away right away means 'most' never came out together, so there is no holiness. Leaving the limbs counts as most coming out, so they need burial.

phrases.english: That is indeed what it is saying:
phrases.notes: He means the משנה's later clause is explaining its first case.

phrases.english: In what case is this said?
With one who cuts and throws away,
phrases.notes: He throws each limb to the dogs before most of the animal has come out.

phrases.english: but one who cuts and leaves –
it becomes as if most of it came out,
and it must be buried.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording question from Step 4
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereads the later clause as a limit on the first case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The later clause looked like a separate case that should have been folded into the first
steps.terutzMaskana: The later clause is the משנה's own explanation of when the first ruling applies, which fits רב הונא
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The משנה works with רב הונא's view.

steps.title: רבא asks whether majority applies to limbs
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks a new question: when deciding whether most of the fetus came out, do we follow the majority within each limb or not?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked: Did they follow the majority when it comes to limbs, or did they not follow the majority when it comes to limbs?
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. רבא asks whether 'follow the majority' is used for limbs when deciding if most of the fetus has come out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Holiness depends on most of the fetus coming out. רבא's question is phrased briefly, so it is not yet clear what exact case he means. The next steps try to work that out.

keyTerms.meaning: Asked a question to which the answer is unknown (a בעיא)

phrases.english: Rava asked:
Did they follow the majority with limbs,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ לֹא הָלְכוּ בְּאֵיבָרִין אַחַר הָרוֹב?
phrases.english: or did they not follow the majority with limbs?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new question after the defense of רב הונא is finished
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether 'majority' reasoning is used inside a limb when deciding if most of the fetus came out

steps.title: Trying to define רבא's case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case רבא means and offers a first suggestion: most of the fetus is out, but only because a small part of one limb is counted.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If you say it is where most of the fetus came out, counting a small part of a limb, and his question is: this small part that is outside, do we count it with the majority of the limb, or do we count it with the majority of the fetus?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what exact case רבא is talking about and tries a first possible answer. This sets up the next step, which will reject it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the suggested case, a small part of a limb is outside. Only by counting it does the fetus pass the 'most is out' line. The question would be whether that small piece goes along with its own limb, which is mostly inside, or with the fetus, which is mostly outside.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? A request to define the exact scenario
If you say. Introduces a suggestion that will usually be rejected
Literally 'we throw it'. Here: we count it together with

phrases.english: What is the case?

phrases.aramaic: אִילֵּימָא, כְּגוֹן שֶׁיָּצָא רוֹב בְּמִיעוּט אֵבֶר,
phrases.english: If you say, where most came out including a small part of a limb,
and his question is:
this small part that is outside,
do we count it with the majority of the limb,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ בָּתַר רוּבָּא דְּעוּבָּר שָׁדֵינַן לֵיהּ?
phrases.english: or do we count it with the majority of the fetus?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to pin down the scenario behind רבא's question
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What exact case רבא's question is about

steps.title: That case is too obvious
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the first suggestion: obviously we follow the majority of the fetus, not the majority of one limb, so רבא would not ask about that.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is obvious that we don't ignore the majority of the fetus and follow the majority of a limb!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the case suggested in Step 7. The answer there is obvious, so it cannot be what רבא was asking.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule depends on the whole fetus, so the fetus's majority wins over one limb's majority. Since that is clear, רבא must have meant a different case.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious, so there is nothing to ask

phrases.english: It is obvious that we don't ignore the majority of the fetus,
and follow the majority of a limb!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the case suggested in Step 7
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the first suggested scenario for רבא's question
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The answer in that scenario is obvious, so it cannot be a real question

steps.title: The real case of רבא's question: half out, with most of one limb
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives the correct case: exactly half the fetus came out, and that half includes most of one limb. Does the small piece of that limb still inside count as 'out'?
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the case is where half of the fetus came out, and that half includes most of a limb. רבא is asking: the small part of that limb that is still inside, do we count it together with the majority of the limb, as if it came out?
steps.whatsHappening: After rejecting the first suggestion, the גמרא now explains what רבא really meant. Half the fetus is out, and that half includes most of one limb.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With exactly half out, the fetus is not yet 'mostly out.' But if the small piece of the limb that is still inside gets counted with the rest of that limb, the total goes over half. So רבא's question decides whether the fetus counts as born.

keyTerms.meaning: Half of it (half of the fetus)
To 'throw it after', meaning to count it together with

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא, כְּגוֹן שֶׁיָּצָא חֶצְיוֹ בְּרוֹב אֵבֶר,
phrases.english: Rather, a case where half of it came out, including most of a limb,
and he is asking:
that small part which is still inside,
what is the law? Do we count it along with the majority of the limb?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, כְּגוֹן שֶׁיָּצָא חֶצְיוֹ בְּרוֹב אֵבֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the case rejected in Step 8 with the correct case behind רבא's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבא's case is half the fetus out, with most of one limb included in that half. The question is whether the inner piece of that limb joins the limb's majority.

steps.title: Trying to prove the answer from the משנה's words 'most of it came out'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: 'If most of it came out, it must be buried.' It argues that 'most' cannot be meant literally, because we already know that most is like all.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'If most of it came out, it must be buried.' What does 'most of it' mean? If you say it means literally most of the fetus, didn't we already know that most of something counts like all of it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the משנה as a possible answer to רבא. It is setting up a proof by showing that the plain reading of 'most of it' would teach nothing new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule that most counts like all is already well known. So if the משנה bothers to say 'most of it came out,' it must be teaching something extra. The next step will say what that extra is.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (an opening suggestion that is about to be rejected)
Most of something counts like all of it

phrases.english: Come and hear: if most of it came out,
it must be buried.
phrases.notes: This is the משנה's line about a fetus that counts as already born, so its cut-up pieces need burial.

phrases.english: What is 'most of it'?
If you say literally most of it,

phrases.aramaic: עַד הַשְׁתָּא לָא אַשְׁמְעִינַן דְּרוּבּוֹ כְּכוּלּוֹ?
phrases.english: until now, had we not already been taught that most of something is like all of it?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שָׁמַע: יָצָא רוּבּוֹ – הֲרֵי זֶה יִקָּבֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to settle the question defined in Step 9.
steps.raayaObject: Whether the inner piece of a limb counts with the limb's majority (Step 9).
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה: יצא רובו הרי זה יקבר. Its plain reading would be pointless, because רובו ככולו is already known.

steps.title: So the משנה must mean half out with most of a limb
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes its proof: 'most of it' must describe half the fetus out with most of a limb. That would mean the inner piece of the limb counts as out, answering רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, doesn't it mean a case where half the fetus came out, including most of a limb?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the proof. It says the משנה's 'most of it' must be exactly רבא's case, and the משנה treats it as born.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the משנה calls 'half out with most of a limb' by the name 'most of it,' then the small piece of the limb inside was counted as out. That would answer רבא: yes, we count it with the majority of the limb.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, is it not...? (introduces the only remaining way to read a source)

phrases.english: Rather, is it not
a case where half of it came out, including most of a limb!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לָאו, כְּגוֹן שֶׁיָּצָא חֶצְיוֹ בְּרוֹב אֵבֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the proof that Step 10 set up.
steps.raayaObject: That the inner minority of a limb is counted with that limb's majority.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's יצא רובו, read as referring to half the fetus out with most of a limb.

steps.title: No: the משנה means most out, with only a small part of a limb
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes off the proof. The משנה may be talking about most of the fetus out, while only a small part of some limb came out. It teaches that we follow the fetus's majority, not the limb.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. The משנה means a case where most of the fetus came out, but only a small part of a certain limb came out. It teaches us that we do not ignore the majority of the animal's fetus and go after the limb instead.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof by finding a different new lesson in the משנה. So the משנה does not answer רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 10 said a plain reading of 'most of it' teaches nothing new. Here the גמרא finds something new it could teach: even when one limb is mostly still inside, we still follow the majority of the whole fetus. Since that is the lesson, רבא's half-and-half case stays unanswered.

keyTerms.meaning: It teaches us (the new point of a source)
We do not leave aside, we do not ignore

steps.confusionAlert: Both cases in this sugya mix 'most' and 'part of a limb,' but they are opposites. רבא's case is half the fetus out with most of a limb. The rejection's case is most of the fetus out with only a small part of a limb.
steps.whatToRemember: The proof from the משנה fails. It can be read as teaching that the fetus's overall majority wins over a single limb, so רבא's question about half out with most of a limb remains open.

phrases.aramaic: לָא, כְּגוֹן שֶׁיָּצָא רוּבּוֹ בְּמִיעוּט אֵבֶר,
phrases.english: No, a case where most of it came out, including only a small part of a limb,
and it teaches us
that we do not ignore the majority of the animal's fetus
and go after the limb.
phrases.notes: He means we don't say the fetus is 'still inside' just because most of that one limb is still inside.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, כְּגוֹן שֶׁיָּצָא רוּבּוֹ בְּמִיעוּט אֵבֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of Steps 10-11 by offering another reading of the משנה.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from יצא רובו only. רבא's question itself is not decided.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the only new lesson possible was רבא's case. In fact the משנה can teach that the fetus's overall majority wins even when a limb is mostly inside.

steps.title: רבא asks about a fetus wrapped in palm fiber or a robe
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks: if the fetus was wrapped in palm fiber, or in a robe, so it did not touch the womb directly, is it still a holy בכור?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked: If someone wrapped it in palm fiber, what is the law? If in his robe, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא opens a new question about a בכור. He asks whether a wrapping that keeps the fetus from touching the womb stops it from counting as 'opening the womb'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בכור is holy because it is the first to open its mother's womb (פטר רחם). If the fetus came out wrapped, maybe the wrapping 'opened' the womb and not the fetus. רבא does not answer; he only raises the doubt.

keyTerms.meaning: Asked a question he was unsure about
Palm fiber, the rough netting on a palm tree
'Opening the womb', what makes a firstborn holy

steps.confusionAlert: This is a brand-new topic. The earlier steps were about a fetus that half came out; now the question is whether the fetus itself has to touch the womb as it is born.

phrases.english: Rava asked:
If one wrapped it in palm fiber, what is the law?
phrases.notes: 'It' is the fetus, wrapped while still inside its mother.

phrases.english: In his robe, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new set of questions about בכור, separate from the half-fetus discussion.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does something between the fetus and the womb stop it from counting as opening the womb?

steps.title: רבא asks about a fetus wrapped in its afterbirth
steps.stepSummary: רבא adds another case: what if the fetus came out wrapped in its own afterbirth?
steps.simpleTranslation: If it was wrapped in its afterbirth, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא adds a third wrapping to his list: the fetus's own afterbirth. This sets up the גמרא's objection in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the palm fiber and robe, the afterbirth is something between the fetus and the womb. The question is whether it also blocks the fetus from 'opening the womb'.

keyTerms.meaning: Afterbirth, the sac that comes out with a newborn

phrases.english: In its afterbirth, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another case to רבא's list.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the fetus's own afterbirth count as blocking it from the womb?

steps.title: The afterbirth is the normal way to be born
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: how can that be a question? Coming out in its afterbirth is how animals are normally born.
steps.simpleTranslation: In its afterbirth? That is its normal way!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא's question. Being born in the afterbirth is completely normal, so it cannot be a doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה gave holiness to firstborns that are born the normal way. Since the afterbirth is part of every normal birth, it cannot block the fetus from opening the womb.

phrases.english: In its afterbirth? That is its normal way!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the case asked in step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's question about the fetus's own afterbirth
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Something that is part of every normal birth cannot be a problem, so there is nothing to ask.

steps.title: The real question: another animal's afterbirth
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא corrects the question: רבא meant the afterbirth of a different animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, if it came out in a different afterbirth, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes רבא's question so it makes sense. He was asking about a fetus wrapped in another animal's afterbirth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Another animal's afterbirth is not part of this fetus's normal birth. It might count as a foreign wrapping like palm fiber, or it might count like an afterbirth, which never blocks. That is the real doubt.

phrases.english: Rather, in a different afterbirth, what is the law?
phrases.notes: He means the afterbirth of some other animal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 15 by changing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא asked about the fetus's own afterbirth.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבא asked about another animal's afterbirth, which is not the normal way.

steps.title: רבא asks about a fetus pulled out by hand
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks: if a hand wrapped around the fetus, held it, and pulled it out, is it a בכור?
steps.simpleTranslation: If it wrapped it, held it, and brought it out, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks another case. Here a hand covers the fetus and pulls it out, so the fetus never touches the womb directly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is like the palm fiber, but the 'wrapping' is a hand that also does the pulling. Maybe the fetus did not open the womb by itself, so it would not be holy.

phrases.english: If it wrapped it, held it, and brought it out, what is the law?
phrases.notes: These verbs are feminine, so it's most likely talking about a hand wrapped around the fetus.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another case to רבא's list of wrappings.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a hand pulling the fetus out stop it from counting as opening the womb?

steps.title: If the head already came out, it is obviously holy
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: what case is this? If the head came out first, the fetus already opened the womb, so there is no question.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If it came out head first, it already opened the womb!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what exact case רבא's wrapping questions are about. It points out that if the head came out first, the fetus is already counted as born and holy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the head comes out, the fetus counts as born and has already opened the womb. Any wrapping of the rest of the body after that changes nothing. This sets up the real case in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the details?

phrases.english: What is the case?
phrases.notes: This question goes back to all of רבא's wrapping cases, not just the last one.

phrases.english: If it came out head first, it already opened it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the exact setup of רבא's wrapping questions.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: In what kind of birth could a wrapping make any difference?

steps.title: The case is a fetus born feet first
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: the question is when the fetus came out feet first, and the rest of the body was wrapped before it left.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is where it came out by way of its legs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the real case: the fetus came out feet first. Then the body was wrapped before most of it came out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With feet first, the fetus does not count as born until most of the body is out. If that main part came out wrapped, we truly do not know if the fetus opened the womb. That is why רבא's question is a real doubt.

phrases.english: Rather, where it came out by way of its legs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'what is the case' question of step 18.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The wrapping cases are about a fetus born feet first, wrapped before most of it came out.

steps.title: רבא asks about a weasel that swallowed the fetus
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks: if a weasel swallowed the fetus inside the womb and carried it out, what is the law?
steps.simpleTranslation: If a weasel swallowed it and brought it out, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks an unusual new case. A weasel went into the womb, swallowed the fetus, and came out with it inside.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the fetus is completely inside another animal as it leaves the womb. This sets up the גמרא's objection in the next step.

phrases.english: If a weasel swallowed it and brought it out, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another case to רבא's questions.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is a fetus carried out inside a weasel considered to have opened the womb?

steps.title: The weasel brought it out, not the fetus
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: if the weasel carried it out, obviously the weasel opened the womb, not the fetus.
steps.simpleTranslation: It brought it out? Then it is the weasel that brought it out!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says this case is not a real question. The weasel left the womb, not the fetus, so the fetus clearly did not open the womb.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fetus was hidden inside the weasel and was never 'born' through the womb itself. So it is clearly not a holy בכור, and there is nothing to ask.

phrases.english: It brought it out? But it is the one that brought it out!
phrases.notes: He means the weasel did the coming out, so the fetus never opened the womb itself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the case in step 20.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the weasel carried the fetus out, the fetus obviously did not open the womb, so there is no doubt.

steps.title: The real weasel case: put back and born on its own
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא corrects the case: the weasel swallowed it, took it out, came back in, threw it up inside the womb, and then the fetus came out by itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it swallowed it and brought it out, then brought it back in and threw it up, and it came out on its own. What is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the weasel question. Now the fetus does come out of the womb by itself, but only after it already left once inside the weasel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fetus finally came out on its own, which looks like a normal birth. But the womb was already 'opened' once when the weasel carried it out. The doubt is whether that first exit means this fetus no longer counts as opening the womb.

keyTerms.meaning: Threw it up, vomited it out

steps.whatToRemember: All of רבא's questions ask one thing: must the fetus itself, and not some wrapping, hand or weasel, be what opens the womb for it to be a holy בכור?

phrases.english: Rather, it swallowed it and brought it out,
and brought it back in and threw it up,
and it came out on its own, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 21 by changing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The weasel simply carried the fetus out.
steps.terutzMaskana: The weasel put it back, and the fetus later came out by itself, which is a real doubt.

steps.title: Two wombs joined together: does another animal's fetus open the womb?
steps.stepSummary: A new question: if two animals' wombs were pressed together and a fetus passed from one into the other and then out, does that strange fetus count as 'opening' the second womb?
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone pressed two wombs together, and a fetus came out of one and went into the other, what is the law? Does only an animal's own fetus 'open' its womb, so a fetus that is not its own does not? Or does even a fetus that is not its own also open it?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks another question in his series. If a fetus from one animal passed through a second animal's womb, does that count as opening the second womb, so the second animal's own baby is no longer a בכור?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only the first fetus that 'opens' a womb (פטר רחם) is a בכור. The question is whether 'opening' needs the animal's own fetus, or whether any fetus passing through counts. If any fetus counts, the second animal's real firstborn would come out second and would not be holy.

keyTerms.meaning: opened (the womb), the act that makes a בכור

phrases.english: If one pressed together two wombs,
phrases.notes: He means the openings of two animals' wombs, both about to give birth for the first time, pushed right up against each other.

phrases.english: and a fetus came out of this one and went into that one, what is the law?
Does its own fetus open the womb,
but one that is not its own does not open it,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא דְּלָאו דִּידֵיהּ נָמֵי פָּטַר?
phrases.english: or perhaps one that is not its own also opens it?

steps.triggerLanguage: הִדְבִּיק שְׁנֵי רְחָמִים, וְיָצָא מִזֶּה וְנִכְנַס לָזֶה, מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another unusual birth case, continuing the run of בעיות about what counts as opening the womb.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a fetus that is not the animal's own count as פטר רחם for that animal's womb?

steps.title: The question stays unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא cannot settle רבא's run of questions about unusual births, ending with the two-wombs case, and leaves them as תיקו.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand (unresolved).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the whole list of רבא's questions without an answer: the wrappings, the other animal's afterbirth, the hand, the weasel and the two wombs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תיקו means no proof was found either way. All of רבא's questions about what counts as the fetus itself 'opening the womb' stay undecided, including whether another animal's fetus can open it.

keyTerms.meaning: let it stand: the question stays unresolved

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the question of step 23, and with it the whole series of רבא's questions from step 13, with no resolution.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: All of רבא's questions about what counts as opening the womb, including whether another animal's fetus counts, are left undecided.

steps.title: The womb opening widened: is it the space or the touching that makes it holy?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא asks: if the walls of the womb opening spread so wide that the fetus did not touch them, is it still holy as a בכור?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא asked: If the walls of the womb opening spread apart, what is the law? Does the airspace of the womb make it holy, and that is present here? Or does touching the womb make it holy, and that is missing here?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא asks a new question: what exactly makes the fetus holy, passing through the womb's space or touching its walls?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the fetus both passes through the opening and rubs against its walls. Here the walls are so wide that only the space is involved. If the space is what counts, the fetus is a בכור. If touching is needed, it is not.

keyTerms.meaning: the walls of the womb's opening

phrases.english: Rav Acha asked:
If the walls of the womb opening spread apart, what is the law?
phrases.notes: So wide that the fetus came out without touching them.

phrases.english: Does the airspace of the womb make it holy, and that is present here,
or perhaps contact with the womb makes it holy,
and that is missing here?

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רַב אַחָא: נִפְתְּחוּ כּוֹתְלֵי בֵּית הָרֶחֶם, מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new בעיא about the womb itself, not about the fetus.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the womb's airspace or physical contact with its walls make the בכור holy?
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the basic question behind the next few בעיות: what part of the womb actually does the 'making holy'.

steps.title: What if the womb walls were removed?
steps.stepSummary: מר בר רב אשי asks about a case where the walls of the womb opening were uprooted.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר בר רב אשי asked: If the walls of the womb opening were uprooted, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: מר בר רב אשי asks a question about womb walls that were uprooted. The גמרא will question this wording right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like רב אחא's question, this asks whether the walls must be in their normal state to make the fetus holy. The case is not yet clear, and the next step sharpens it.

keyTerms.meaning: were uprooted, pulled out of place

phrases.english: Mar bar Rav Ashi asked:
If the walls of the womb opening were uprooted, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי מָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי: נֶעְקְרוּ כּוֹתְלֵי בֵּית הָרֶחֶם, מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another question about the condition of the womb walls.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Do uprooted womb walls still make the fetus holy?

steps.title: If the walls are gone, there is nothing to ask
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: if the walls were uprooted, they are simply not there, so of course they cannot make the fetus holy.
steps.simpleTranslation: If they were uprooted, they are not there!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the question. If the walls are gone, there is clearly nothing to make the fetus holy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The objection says the case as worded is obvious, so it cannot be a real question. This forces the גמרא to describe the case in a way that is actually in doubt.

phrases.english: If they were uprooted, they are not there!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of מר בר רב אשי's question.
steps.kashyaTarget: The case of uprooted womb walls in step 26
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Walls that are gone obviously cannot make the fetus holy, so there is no question.

steps.title: Walls moved out of place and lying on the fetus's neck
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא redefines the case: the walls came loose and lay on the fetus's neck as it came out. Do walls make it holy only in their normal place, or even out of place?
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the case is where they came loose and lay on its neck. What is the law? Do they make it holy only in their place, and not when out of their place? Or perhaps they make it holy even when out of their place?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the objection by changing the case. The walls are still there, only out of their normal spot, resting on the fetus's neck.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the walls really do touch the fetus, so the question is a fair one. The doubt is whether the walls must be in their natural position to make the fetus holy, or whether touching them anywhere is enough.

phrases.english: Rather, they came loose and lay on it,
on its neck. What is the law?
Do they make it holy when in their place,
but not when out of their place,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא שֶׁלֹּא בִּמְקוֹמָן נָמֵי מְקַדְּשִׁי?
phrases.english: or perhaps they make it holy even when out of their place?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא נֶעְקְרוּ וְתָלוּ לֵיהּ בְּצַוְּארֵיהּ, מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 27 by restating the case so it is a real doubt.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The walls were completely gone, which would make the question pointless.
steps.terutzMaskana: The walls came loose but were still present on the fetus's neck. The doubt is whether walls out of their normal place still make it holy.
steps.confusionAlert: The question is not left as 'walls that disappeared.' After the אלא, the walls are still touching the fetus, only in the wrong spot.

steps.title: What if the womb walls were thinned?
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה asks רבי זירא: if the walls of the womb opening became thin, is the fetus still holy?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה asked רבי זירא: If the walls of the womb opening were thinned, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה asks a new question about womb walls that have been made thinner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the walls are still in place, but part of their thickness is missing. The question is whether a reduced wall still counts as the womb that makes the fetus a בכור.

keyTerms.meaning: were thinned, partly worn or cut away

phrases.aramaic: בָּעֵי מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה מֵרַבִּי זֵירָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya asked Rabbi Zeira:
If the walls of the womb opening were thinned, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה מֵרַבִּי זֵירָא: נִגְמְמוּ כּוֹתְלֵי בֵּית הָרֶחֶם, מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another בעיא about damaged womb walls.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Do thinned womb walls still make the fetus holy?

steps.title: רבי זירא: you touched on a question we already asked
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא replies that this question connects to a question that was already raised before him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: You have touched on a question that was already asked before us.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא starts to answer by linking רבי ירמיה's question to an earlier one. He is setting up a quote of that earlier question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of answering directly, רבי זירא shows that the thinned-walls case belongs to a bigger question about a partly damaged womb opening. That earlier discussion will help decide the new case.

phrases.english: He said to him: You have touched
on a question that was already asked before us,

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: קָא נָגְעַתְּ בְּבַעְיָא דְּאִיבַּעְיָא לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to רבי ירמיה's question by pointing to an earlier question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The thinned-walls case is tied to an earlier question about a partly broken womb opening.

steps.title: The earlier question: a womb opening partly broken away
steps.stepSummary: The quoted earlier question: if most of the opening is intact and the fetus left through the broken part, or most is broken and it left through the intact part, what is the law?
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי זירא asked, and some say רבי זירא asked רבי אסי: If the standing part is larger than the broken part, and the fetus came out through the broken part; or if the broken part is larger than the standing part, and it came out through the standing part, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the earlier question that רבי זירא mentioned. It is about a womb opening that is partly broken away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two cases pull in opposite directions. In one, most of the wall is intact but the fetus went through the missing part. In the other, most of the wall is missing but the fetus went through the intact part. The doubt is whether we follow the majority of the wall or the exact spot the fetus touched.

phrases.english: As Rabbi Zeira asked,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי זֵירָא מֵרַבִּי אַסִּי:
phrases.english: and some say Rabbi Zeira asked Rabbi Asi:
If the standing part is larger than the broken part,
phrases.notes: This is talking about the walls of the womb opening, where a section was cut away.

phrases.english: and it came out through the broken part;
or if the broken part is larger than the standing part,
and it came out through the standing part, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּבָעֵי רַבִּי זֵירָא, וְאָמְרִי לַהּ בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי זֵירָא מֵרַבִּי אַסִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Quotes the earlier בעיא that רבי זירא said the new question touches on.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: When the womb opening is partly broken, do we follow the majority of the wall or the spot the fetus actually passed through?
steps.whyThisMatters: Thinned walls are like walls that are partly missing, so how this question is decided shapes the answer to רבי ירמיה's case.

steps.title: The earlier question only applied when some wall was still standing
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא explains that the earlier question about a mostly broken opening was only asked because part of the wall still stood. When the walls were thinned away, it is obvious the fetus is not holy, so nobody asked.
steps.simpleTranslation: That earlier question was only asked when the broken part is bigger than the standing part, because at least some standing wall still exists. But when the walls were thinned away, nobody asked, because the answer is obvious.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא now shows how the earlier question answers רבי ירמיה. The earlier question was only raised because some wall was still standing, so thinned walls were never in doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the case of פרוץ מרובה על העומד there is still some real wall left, so it is possible that wall could make the fetus holy. That is why it was worth asking. With thinned walls there is no standing part at all, so it is obvious the fetus is not made holy, and that answers רבי ירמיה.

keyTerms.meaning: The question was only asked up to here: it was limited to this case
The broken part is bigger than the standing part
The standing, still-whole part of the wall

steps.whatToRemember: A wall that is mostly broken can still raise a question, because some of it is standing. Thinned walls have nothing standing, so the fetus is clearly not made holy. That is the answer to רבי ירמיה.

phrases.english: That question was only asked
about a case where the broken part is more than the standing part
since at least some standing part still exists
but where the walls were thinned
the question was not asked
phrases.notes: Nobody needed to ask, because with nothing left standing, the fetus is clearly not made holy.

steps.triggerLanguage: עַד כָּאן לָא אִיבַּעְיָא לֵיהּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the earlier question quoted in step 31 settles רבי ירמיה's question from step 29.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Thinned walls do not make the fetus holy. The earlier question only came up because some wall was standing, and here nothing is left standing.
